hints: Focus on the two big assumptions of an ideal gas, that particles have no volume and have zero attraction for each other.
Compare the four gases for polarity and intermolecular forces, noting that one of them can form hydrogen bonds between its molecules.
Link the strongest intermolecular attractions to being closest to liquefying at room conditions, which means the largest departure from ideal behaviour.
walkthrough:
**Recall What Makes a Gas Ideal**

An ideal gas is a perfect model where particles are point masses with no intermolecular forces. Real gases deviate most when molecules attract each other strongly or are large and polarisable.

Assumptions broken: $$\text{no intermolecular forces, negligible molecular volume}$$

**Compare Forces in the Four Gases**

$\text{H}_2$ and $\text{Ne}$ are tiny and non-polar with only very weak London forces, so they are very close to ideal. $\text{CO}_2$ is larger with more electrons, so it has stronger London forces, but it is non-polar overall.

**Spot the Strongest Attraction**

$\text{NH}_3$ is polar and has N-H bonds, so it forms hydrogen bonds between molecules. This is much stronger than London forces alone, pulls molecules together, and makes it the easiest to liquefy and the least ideal under room conditions.

options.A: CO2 does deviate more than H2 and Ne because it is larger with stronger London forces, but it is non-polar with no hydrogen bonding, so its deviation is smaller than for ammonia.
options.B: H2 is very small with very weak London forces and a very low boiling point, so it behaves very nearly as an ideal gas at room temperature and pressure.
options.C: Ne is a tiny noble gas atom with only extremely weak London forces and no polarity, so it is one of the closest to ideal behaviour, not the most deviating.
options.D: NH3 is polar and exhibits hydrogen bonding, the strongest intermolecular force here. These strong attractions cause the greatest deviation from the no-attraction ideal gas model under room conditions.
